summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9–10) learn the relative sizes of units within one system (metric km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml; and time units hr/min/sec, which are not metric) and convert between metric units, expressing a measurement in a smaller unit and recording equivalents in conversion tables. Metric conversion is applied place value: converting to a SMALLER unit means multiplying (there are more of them); converting to a LARGER unit means dividing (there are fewer of them). The two persistent hazards are choosing the wrong operation and manipulating zeros/decimals mechanically ('add a zero') instead of moving the digits across a fixed decimal point. The core activity is a live place-value transformation where digits slide across a fixed point, supported by table-building, mixed-unit recomposition, and targeted practice that probes direction and zero errors. (Note: the digit-sliding by 10/100/1000 applies to the metric units; hr/min/sec relate by ×60 and are included only in the 'relative sizes' knowledge.)
misconceptions: Confuses when to multiply and when to divide (converts to a smaller unit by dividing, or vice versa).
'Adds a zero' or manipulates zeros mechanically, which breaks with decimals (3.5 km → '350 m' or '3.50 m' instead of 3500 m).
Treats a mixed unit as concatenation (2 kg 35 g → '235 g'), a two-separate-numbers error.
Fills a conversion table by copying a pattern without understanding the ×10 relationship.

activities.title: Slide the digits across a fixed decimal point
steps: Enter a measurement such as 3.5 km and choose the target unit (metres).
Before computing, answer the prompt: 'Is a metre bigger or smaller than a kilometre — so will there be MORE metres or FEWER?' State whether this means multiply or divide.

Watch (or physically move, using a place-value chart or Gattegno chart) every digit slide three places left while the decimal point stays nailed in place, so 3.5 becomes 3500, with place-holder zeros dropping in where needed.
Repeat for a case that keeps the decimal visible, e.g. 1.75 km to m, naming where each digit lands (the 1 becomes 1 thousand, giving 1750 m).
Do at least one divide case too, e.g. 4500 m to km, moving digits three places right to give 4.5 km.
activities.insight: The number grows (or shrinks) because the DIGITS move a fixed number of places, not because zeros are 'added' — so 3.5 km can never become 3.50 m.

activities.title: Build and check conversion tables
steps: Complete a cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__ and say what you multiply by for each row.
Read the completed table aloud as a set of equivalent multiplications ('each centimetre is ten millimetres — I'm multiplying by 10').
Check each row against the ×10 relationship and flag any row that breaks the pattern, explaining why it is wrong.
Build a second table for a different pair of units (e.g. kg→g, ×1000) to see the same structure with a different multiplier.
activities.insight: A conversion table is a repeated multiplication by the same factor, not a copied number pattern — understanding the factor lets you extend or correct any row.

activities.title: Recompose a mixed unit into one smaller unit
steps: Express 2 kg 350 g as a number of grams, showing the step 2 kg = 2000 g, then 2000 + 350 = 2350 g.
Test the tricky case 2 kg 35 g: decide whether it equals 235 g or 2035 g and justify using place value.
Use a bar (2 kg + loose grams recomposed as one quantity) to make the missing hundreds place visible when the loose amount is small.
State a check: the combined gram total must include the thousands from the kilograms.
activities.insight: A mixed unit is recomposed by converting the larger part and ADDING, not by writing the two numbers side by side — so 2 kg 35 g = 2035 g, not 235 g.

activities.title: Choose and justify the operation before calculating
steps: For a mix of conversions (some to smaller units, some to larger), first state 'multiply' or 'divide' and why, using unit size, BEFORE working the answer.
Answer true/false checks that target the zero error, e.g. 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' and explain.
For each worked conversion, say aloud 'did I multiply or divide, and how did I know?'
activities.insight: The operation follows from which unit is bigger and how many of the smaller unit fit in it — the heuristic 'fewer of the bigger unit → divide' decides direction every time.

checkQuestion: Give the child three tasks and ask them to think aloud: (1) 'Convert 3.5 km to metres.' (2) 'Complete this cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__.' (3) 'Write 2 kg 350 g as a number of grams.' Each time ask 'did you multiply or divide, and how did you know?' Watch the direction reasoning and how they handle the digits/zeros — not just the answers.
checkAnswer: 3.5 km = 3500 m (×1000, reasoning 'metres are smaller so there are more'); table 10, 20, 50, 100; 2 kg 350 g = 2350 g (2000 + 350). Chooses the operation from unit size and moves the digits correctly rather than appending zeros.
